comparedAgainst: https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/dsa/recursion/ (base case / recursive case, sum-of-naturals, factorial and Fibonacci examples, generic stack-frame description, stack-overflow warning; no filesystem example, no tail-call discussion)
https://www.programiz.com/c-programming/c-recursion (single sum-of-naturals example plus a mirror analogy; no call-stack detail, no stack-overflow measurement, no tail calls)

https://www.freecodecamp.org/news/understanding-recursion-in-programming/ (broad survey: string reversal, palindrome, base conversion, binary search, Fibonacci, merge sort, linked lists, BST, DFS, with animated stack-frame walkthroughs; lists tail-call recursion as a topic but does not verify it; no filesystem example)

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/fsharp/language-reference/functions/recursive-functions-the-rec-keyword (the closest thing to a primary-source tail-call discussion on learn.microsoft.com: explains F#'s rec keyword, tail recursion and the TailCall attribute, but for F#, at the language level, with no IL inspection and no claim about what C#/the JIT actually does)
justification: Target queries 'recursion explained' / 'recursion in C#'. Caveat on method: this session's WebSearch quota was exhausted before this review started (already spent by other work), so originality was checked by WebFetching four commonly-cited pages directly (GeeksforGeeks' general recursion page, Programiz's C recursion page, freeCodeCamp's recursion guide, and Microsoft's F# tail-recursion doc as the closest primary-source tail-call treatment) and reading their content and phrasing back, rather than running exact-phrase SERP searches for stolen sentences. Within that constraint, none of the four uses a filesystem/DirectorySize example, none instruments a recursive function to print an indented call/return trace the way the Factorial section does, none builds a recursion-tree diagram from an actual Dictionary-based call counter the way the Fibonacci section does, and critically none does what this article's tail-call section does: write a self-recursive accumulator function, read its own compiled assembly back via System.Reflection.Metadata, and scan the IL bytes for the FE 14 tail. prefix to show Roslyn did not emit it, then separately measure debug vs. release crash depth to show the JIT did not turn the call into a loop either. That is a materially deeper, more rigorous treatment of 'does C# optimize tail calls' than any blog post or tutorial commonly given for this query, which typically just assert 'C# does not guarantee TCO' without proof. The DirectorySize opening is a genuine, own hook (built, measured, and torn down in the sample itself, not a static array); Factorial and Fibonacci are the two examples every recursion tutorial reaches for, and the writer's front matter/outline says so openly by using them for the standard purposes (stack trace, overlapping subproblems) rather than trying to pretend they are novel -- that is honest reuse of well-worn worked examples in service of an original overall structure, not the copying the brief prohibits. Permutations (choose-recurse-undo, with the 'forgot to undo the swap' bug) and the explicit-Stack<T> rewrite are also not reused from any of the four comparison pages' running examples. Fabrication check: all four front-matter sources were fetched and re-read against the article's exact quotations -- StackOverflowException ('cannot be caught with a try/catch block, and the corresponding process is terminated by default') matches learn.microsoft.com verbatim; the Thread(ThreadStart,Int32) remarks ('the most likely cause is programming error, such as infinite recursion' and the 1-megabyte default) match verbatim (article's bracketed '[of stack problems]' is an honest editorial insertion into an otherwise exact quote); OpCodes.Tailcall's 'the current method's stack frame should be removed before the call instruction is executed' matches verbatim, as does the FE 14 / tail. hex-and-mnemonic pairing; the dotnet/runtime 'Tail call JIT conditions' doc does say the 64-bit JIT tail-calls 'whenever we're allowed to' and does list return-type mismatches, disqualifying value-type parameter sizes, synchronized methods and address-taken locals among its disqualifying conditions, all correctly summarized. All four listed sources are cited inline at the exact point their claim is made (100% citation rate, a clean example of the pilot-round lesson binary-search's round 1 was marked down for). No filler: opens with a content-bearing sentence about directory size, no 'in today's world'/'let's dive in'/'in this article' boilerplate, no 'Exercises' H2 with a giveaway first item (exercises are woven in at four different points, forms vary as claimed: extend-it/memoize, find-the-bug, predict-then-check, extend-it/count-directories), no conclusion-that-repeats-headings, no ad code or ad placeholders. Toolchain statement ('Measured with .NET 10.0.401 on Windows 11, x64') sits at the start of the stack-overflow section, the first place a measured number appears, exactly as the writer claims and exactly as the brief's binding lesson requires -- not a stamped opening sentence. Exercise solutions are all collapsed behind ':::solution' with no output panel exposed in the question for the 'predict-then-check' exercise (Sum(5000)); the 'find-the-bug' permutations exercise states as given only that 'six lines still come out' (necessary scaffolding to pose the interesting question of which permutations are wrong, not the answer to it), which is a lighter touch than the binary-search sibling's own find-the-bug exercise, where the buggy program's actual output is printed in the question itself -- so this article is at least as careful about not leaking answers as its shipped sibling. Structural variety against binary-search.md (shape D, debugging story: opens with a subtly wrong function, derives an invariant, fixes it) is real and by design: recursion.md is shape W per CONTENT_PLAN.md, opens with a correct worked example (DirectorySize) and only reaches theory afterward; headings on both articles are content-specific with no shared template, no repeated 'Three things/ways' tic, no boilerplate Introduction/Conclusion. Boundary with complexity/analyzing-loops-and-recursion.md (not yet published) is handled honestly: the one sentence that could have linked to it ('Analyzing the Complexity of Loops and Recursion, a companion article...') is left as plain italic text, not a markdown link, and docs/crosslinks/algorithms/recursion.md records the exact anchor, target route and paragraph for the integrator to wire later, matching what is actually in the body. The article never performs the recurrence/Master-theorem analysis that companion article owns; it only shows the shape of the repeated fib(2) call, which is the honest boundary the writer claims. `node tools/run-code.mjs` reports PASS, blocks=24, executed=12, matching the brief. Why not higher: one unsourced generalization ('Factorial makes both cases explicit, which is why it is the standard first example') asserts a pedagogical convention without support, the kind of 'what most people/tutorials do' claim the brief's pilot lessons flag; and originality was verified by WebFetch against four representative pages rather than a live search for lifted phrasing, so a small residual risk of undetected close paraphrasing elsewhere on the web remains that a full-budget search pass would close out.
